question: A telecom company is launching a generative AI assistant on Vertex AI that answers customer questions using retrieval from internal billing documents. A security review must address prompt injection through retrieved content, leakage of customer PII in responses, and exfiltration of the vector store and training data to outside projects. Which controls should you include in the design? (Choose three.)
options: Screen prompts, retrieved context and model responses with Model Armor templates configured for prompt injection, jailbreak and sensitive data detection.
Grant the assistant's Cloud Run service account the Editor role on the project so that it can access all required Vertex AI and storage resources.
Use Sensitive Data Protection to inspect and de-identify PII in the document corpus before it is indexed, and to inspect responses for residual PII.
Store the Gemini API key in the frontend JavaScript so the browser can call the model directly and reduce backend latency.
Place the project in a VPC Service Controls perimeter with Vertex AI, Cloud Storage and BigQuery as restricted services to prevent data movement to outside projects.
Disable Cloud Audit Logs for Vertex AI to avoid recording customer prompts in logs.
explanation: Model Armor addresses prompt injection and jailbreak (including attacks embedded in retrieved documents) and can flag sensitive data in prompts and responses; Sensitive Data Protection reduces the PII that can leak by de-identifying the corpus and screening outputs; and VPC Service Controls prevents exfiltration of the vector store and data to projects outside the perimeter. Option B violates least privilege; the service account should have narrowly scoped Vertex AI and storage roles. Option D exposes credentials to end users. Option F removes the audit trail needed for security investigations; sensitive prompt content should be handled with log field redaction or exclusion rather than disabling audit logs.
hint: Core Rule (Securing generative AI applications): Model Armor addresses prompt injection and jailbreak (including attacks embedded in retrieved documents) and can flag sensitive data in prompts and responses; Sensitive Data Protection reduces the PII that can leak by de-identifying the corpus and screening outputs; and VPC Service Controls prevents exfiltration of the vector store and data to projects outside the perimeter.

question: An engineering firm is building an internal knowledge assistant with Vertex AI Agent Builder that answers questions from documents stored in Google Drive and Cloud Storage. Documents carry existing per-user and per-group access restrictions. The firm requires that the assistant never surfaces content in an answer that the requesting employee is not already permitted to read, and that this be enforced by the platform rather than by prompt instructions. What should you do?
options: Index all documents into a single data store and instruct the model in the system prompt to check the user's department before answering.

Configure the Vertex AI Search data store with access control enabled, connecting the identity provider so that document ACLs are ingested, and pass the end user's identity with each search or answer request so that results are filtered to documents the user can access.
Create one data store per department and route each user's questions to their department's data store based on their email domain.
Apply Sensitive Data Protection to redact confidential sections from all documents before indexing so that no restricted content can be retrieved.
explanation: Vertex AI Search supports access-control-aware data stores that ingest document ACLs from sources like Google Drive and Cloud Storage; when the end user's identity is passed with the request, retrieval is filtered to documents that user is authorized to view, providing platform-level enforcement. Option A relies on prompt instructions, which the requirement excludes and which can be bypassed. Option C is coarse-grained, ignores per-user and per-document restrictions, and does not handle cross-department access. Option D destroys legitimate content for authorized users and does not model per-user permissions.
hint: Core Rule (Secure AI retrieval): Vertex AI Search supports access-control-aware data stores that ingest document ACLs from sources like Google Drive and Cloud Storage; when the end user's identity is passed with the request, retrieval is filtered to documents that user is authorized to view, providing platform-level enforcement.

question: A startup shipped a mobile app that calls a Gemini model directly using a Google Cloud API key embedded in the app binary. The key was extracted and abused, generating a large unexpected bill. The startup needs to stop the abuse and redesign the integration so that credentials are never exposed to client devices, while keeping the app's functionality. What should you do?
options: Rotate the API key, obfuscate it in the next app release, and set a billing budget alert.
Rotate the API key and restrict it to the app's bundle identifier and to the Vertex AI API only, leaving the key in the app.

Move Gemini calls to a backend service such as Cloud Run that authenticates with its own service account, and have the app call the backend with end-user authentication (for example Firebase Authentication and App Check); then delete the leaked key.
Switch the app to a service account JSON key stored in the app's encrypted preferences instead of an API key.
explanation: Credentials embedded in client applications can always be extracted, so the recommended design is to keep model credentials on a trusted backend that uses its attached service account, and to authenticate end users to that backend with an identity solution plus App Check to limit abuse. Option A is security through obscurity and a budget alert only detects abuse after the fact. Option B reduces but does not remove the risk, because application restrictions can be spoofed and the key remains extractable. Option D replaces one extractable secret with a more powerful one.
hint: Core Rule (API credential security): Credentials embedded in client applications can always be extracted, so the recommended design is to keep model credentials on a trusted backend that uses its attached service account, and to authenticate end users to that backend with an identity solution plus App Check to limit abuse.

question: A software company uses Cloud Build to build and deploy to production. Audit findings note that the default Cloud Build service account has broad project permissions, that build logs are viewable by all developers, and that any developer who can edit the repository can change the build configuration to deploy anywhere. The company wants to reduce the blast radius of a compromised repository or pipeline. What should you do?
options: Configure each production trigger to run with a dedicated user-managed service account holding only the roles needed for that deployment, store build configurations in a protected branch with required reviews, and use private worker pools with restricted logging where required.
Grant the default Cloud Build service account the Owner role so that builds never fail on permissions, and rely on repository access control for security.
Move all builds to developers' laptops so that the Cloud Build service account is no longer needed.
Disable Cloud Build audit logging to hide deployment details from developers.
explanation: Cloud Build triggers can run as user-managed service accounts, allowing least-privilege, per-pipeline identities so a compromised trigger cannot deploy outside its scope; protecting the branch that holds build configuration prevents unilateral changes, and private pools and log access controls address exposure of sensitive build output. Option B expands the blast radius. Option C removes the auditable, isolated build environment and typically worsens supply chain security. Option D reduces visibility for security teams rather than reducing risk.
hint: Core Rule (Cloud Build security): Cloud Build triggers can run as user-managed service accounts, allowing least-privilege, per-pipeline identities so a compromised trigger cannot deploy outside its scope; protecting the branch that holds build configuration prevents unilateral changes, and private pools and log access controls address exposure of sensitive build output.

question: A fintech company wants its Cloud Build pipeline to fail automatically when a newly built container image contains a vulnerability of severity CRITICAL, before the image is tagged as release-ready and pushed to the production repository. The team prefers Google-managed tooling. What should you do?
options: Push the image to production first and rely on Artifact Registry's automatic scanning to email the team when critical CVEs are found.
Add a manual approval step in Cloud Build where a security engineer checks the vulnerability report in the console.

Add a Cloud Build step that uses the Artifact Analysis On-Demand Scanning API (gcloud artifacts docker images scan) on the locally built image and fails the build if any CRITICAL vulnerability is returned.
Enable Web Security Scanner in Security Command Center and configure it to scan the image before the push step.
explanation: On-Demand Scanning lets a pipeline scan a local or registry image synchronously with Artifact Analysis and inspect the results, so a build step can enforce a severity threshold before the image is promoted. Option D is wrong because Web Security Scanner tests running web applications, not container images.
hint: Core Rule (Vulnerability gating in CI): On-Demand Scanning lets a pipeline scan a local or registry image synchronously with Artifact Analysis and inspect the results, so a build step can enforce a severity threshold before the image is promoted.

question: A healthcare company is preparing a new GKE Standard cluster for production workloads that handle patient data. The security team wants to block privileged containers and hostPath mounts across all application namespaces, ensure nodes boot only verified software with rootkit protection, and remove all reliance on node service account credentials by pods. Which actions should you take? (Choose three.)
options: Enable Shielded GKE Nodes with Secure Boot and integrity monitoring on the node pools.
Enforce Pod Security Standards at the restricted or baseline level with Pod Security Admission, or use Policy Controller constraints, on application namespaces.
Grant the node service account the Editor role so that pods have any permission they may need.
Enable Workload Identity Federation for GKE and configure GKE Metadata Server so that pods cannot reach the node's metadata credentials.
Run all application pods in the kube-system namespace so that they inherit the cluster's system security policies.
Disable Cloud Logging on the cluster to avoid storing patient data in logs.
explanation: Shielded GKE Nodes provide verified boot and integrity monitoring; Pod Security Admission or Policy Controller enforces the Pod Security Standards that forbid privileged containers and hostPath; and Workload Identity Federation for GKE, through the GKE metadata server, gives pods their own identities while blocking access to the node service account credentials. Option C is the opposite of least privilege. Option E is an anti-pattern that mixes application workloads with system components and does not add policy enforcement. Option F removes observability and audit capability; sensitive data should be handled with log redaction and access control rather than disabling logging.
hint: Core Rule (GKE hardening): Shielded GKE Nodes provide verified boot and integrity monitoring; Pod Security Admission or Policy Controller enforces the Pod Security Standards that forbid privileged containers and hostPath; and Workload Identity Federation for GKE, through the GKE metadata server, gives pods their own identities while blocking access to the node service account credentials.
